title: Dispute Resolution / Termination / Contract Exit | Procurement Journey

logical_structure.title: Principles for Managing Disputes and Termination
Key Components of the Exit Plan

content_blocks.text: This guidance supports organisations to manage disputes, potential contract failure, termination, and contract exit in medium- to high-risk contracts.
Minimise disruption to service users and operational teams
Provide a consistent, defensible approach supported by audit evidence
Principles for Managing Disputes and Termination
heading_path: Principles for Managing Disputes and Termination

content_blocks.text: Proportionality – Medium and high-risk contracts require early visibility of risks, structured escalation, and robust documentation.
heading_path: Principles for Managing Disputes and Termination

content_blocks.text: Fairness & transparency – All decisions must be well-evidenced and communicated clearly.
heading_path: Principles for Managing Disputes and Termination

content_blocks.text: Continuity of public service – Any dispute or termination process must prioritise maintaining service delivery and safeguarding citizens.
heading_path: Principles for Managing Disputes and Termination

content_blocks.text: Collaboration first – Formal escalation and termination should only occur after reasonable attempts at resolution.
heading_path: Principles for Managing Disputes and Termination

content_blocks.text: Legal compliance – Seek legal guidance early in cases involving severe breach, financial loss, or risk to people.
heading_path: Principles for Managing Disputes and Termination
Principles for Managing Disputes and Termination

content_blocks.text: Contract management arrangements should identify what happens when the contract is not being delivered as agreed or, the agreed quality standards are not being met.
heading_path: Principles for Managing Disputes and Termination

content_blocks.text: Performance issues should be addressed immediately, and escalated within the supplier's organisation if not resolved promptly.
heading_path: Principles for Managing Disputes and Termination

content_blocks.text: If you find that the supplier is not delivering the agreed level of service, you should raise this with them immediately. For quickness, this can be done by telephone but should be followed up in writing. The supplier should be asked for an action plan to ensure that the required levels of service re-commence in a short time frame. Depending on the severity of the issue, it may also be necessary to hold a face-to-face meeting with the supplier. All discussions/meetings, etc. should be minuted to ensure an audit trail exists. If resolution of the issue is not completed within the timescales agreed then the issue should be escalated (see below) and your Organisation’s procurement contact notified of the problem;
heading_path: Principles for Managing Disputes and Termination

content_blocks.text: If the issue(s) raised are not resolved to your satisfaction, they should be escalated within the supplier's organisation. An early face-to-face meeting should be arranged where actions and timescales to remedy the situation should be agreed and implemented. The recovery actions should be monitored on a regular basis to ensure that the agreed recovery/ resolution dates do not slip. All discussions/ agreements should be noted in writing;
heading_path: Principles for Managing Disputes and Termination

content_blocks.text: Contract Managers/ Contract Management Officers should ensure the escalation process is clearly defined, understood and communicated to all stakeholders and end users.
heading_path: Principles for Managing Disputes and Termination

heading_path: Principles for Managing Disputes and Termination
